title: One sound, two fates
lede: 刺客 and 資格 are pronounced exactly the same: shikaku. Drag the slider below to watch one word turn into the other, just as the heroine does.
morphLabel: Morph 刺客 into 資格
morphHint: Drag, use left/right arrows, or press play.

chars.m: to stab, pierce; also a thorn

pairs.note: Literally 'a person who comes to stab'. A classical-sounding word for a hired killer, more poetic than {{g:koroshiya|殺し屋}}.
Resources that meet a standard. Used in phrases like 'having no right to…'. This is Shikaku's feeling at the climax.

wordplay: The official title is written in {{g:katakana|シカク}}, not kanji. Katakana records only sound, so Japanese readers hear 'shikaku' without being told which kanji is meant. The heroine's name and the story's big question become the same word {{tag:fact}}.

At the start she is 刺客: a professional who comes to stab. At the end, what she questions is 資格: whether she has the right to love. Her arc is the journey from the first kanji to the second {{tag:fan}}.
Neither English nor Indonesian has a word that holds both meanings at once. That is why the official translation keeps the name 'Shikaku': the wordplay can be explained, but not translated.
homophonesNote: Japanese has many homophones. Those below are not officially part of the title; they are a fan reading.
